questions.q: Heating dry benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate gives fluorobenzene along with:
questions.explain: The aryl cation formed on loss of N₂ takes F⁻ from BF₄⁻, leaving BF₃. So the by-products are N₂ and BF₃, and the fluorine in ArF comes from the counter-ion.

questions.q: Which reagent sequence converts benzenediazonium chloride into fluorobenzene?
options: HBF₄, then heat the dried precipitate
questions.explain: HBF₄ precipitates C₆H₅N₂⁺BF₄⁻, which decomposes on heating to C₆H₅F. Copper fluorides do not give aryl fluorides in a Sandmeyer-type reaction.

questions.q: Why can benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate be filtered and dried, while benzenediazonium chloride is used only in cold solution?
options: The tetrafluoroborate is insoluble in water and stable at room temperature
The tetrafluoroborate is a covalent compound with no N₂⁺ group
BF₄⁻ oxidises any free aniline present
The chloride is insoluble and precipitates too fast
questions.explain: ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻ precipitates from water and is stable at room temperature, so it can be isolated. The chloride decomposes easily and can explode when dry.

questions.q: Which statement about the mechanism of the Balz–Schiemann reaction is correct?
options: It is a copper-catalysed radical reaction, like the Sandmeyer reaction
Fluoride attacks the ring first and N₂ leaves afterwards in an addition–elimination path
It is believed to go through an aryl cation formed on loss of N₂, with no copper needed
BF₃ is the fluorinating agent and BF₄⁻ is a spectator
questions.explain: Heat breaks the C–N bond, N₂ leaves, and the aryl cation captures F⁻ from BF₄⁻ (an SN1-like path). The Sandmeyer reaction is the copper-catalysed radical route, and BF₃ is a by-product, not the reagent.
